situations.title: Delivering bad news to your manager
situations.context: A project is going to miss its date, a client is unhappy, or a mistake you made will cost time or money, and your manager does not know yet. The pull is to wait until you have fixed it or until the picture is clearer, but late news is what damages trust. Raising problems upward also feels risky, so people soften the message until the problem gets lost.
situations.goal: Your manager hears the problem early and plainly, understands what it means for them, and leaves with options and a next step, trusting your reporting more than before.

approach.step: Tell them early, before decisions lock in
approach.detail: Raise the problem as soon as you know it is real, not once you have solved it. Bosses need bad news in time to act, and concerns raised before plans are locked in are received better than late ones.

approach.step: Shape the message as What, So What, Now What
approach.detail: Write one sentence on what happened, one on what it means for this manager (dates, money, the client), and one on what you propose. Saying what you would do next makes it more likely they will act on it, and less likely you will be seen as just complaining.

approach.step: Match the format to how your manager takes in information
approach.detail: If your manager likes to read first, send a short note and then talk. If they prefer to hear things, talk first and send the written version afterward. Either way, ask for a private slot with enough time rather than dropping it into a group meeting. Propose a specific time and length rather than 'Got a second?'.

approach.step: Signal the news, then say it plainly
approach.detail: Open with a short warning that you have a problem to share, then state it in plain words without padding or jokes. A joke attached to an admission makes listeners take it less seriously, and here you need them to. Skip the small-talk cushion: 'This won't be easy to hear,' then the main point within your first two sentences.

approach.step: Let the reaction land before moving to the plan
approach.detail: If your manager is frustrated or worried, acknowledge it briefly and give them a moment before you go into options. If the news is big, do not push for every decision in the same sitting; agree what has to be decided now and what can wait.

approach.step: Offer options and ask what you are missing
approach.detail: Lay out one or two realistic ways forward, including a small test if that fits, and then ask what they know that you do not. Your manager may have context from above that changes the best option.

approach.step: Follow up in writing and set the next update
approach.detail: Send the key facts, options and agreed next steps in a short note so nobody has to rely on memory, and say when they will hear from you next.

example_wording: Can I get fifteen minutes today? There is a problem on the Henderson launch that I want you to hear from me first.
The short version: we will miss the March 3 date by about two weeks, which puts the client demo at risk. I see two ways to win back part of that and want your call on which.
What am I missing? Is there anything on your side that changes how you would handle this?
I will send you a short note with the dates and both options by end of day, and update you Thursday either way.
pitfalls: Waiting until you have a full fix, so your manager hears it from someone else first
Opening with so much background that it is unclear there is a problem at all
Joking about it or minimizing it, which makes the problem sound smaller than it is
Bringing only the problem, with no proposed next step
Pushing for every decision in the first conversation while your manager is still reacting
situations.evidence_note: The strongest support is the High-confidence research on why people stay silent with superiors (morrison-2014-voice-01); the other insights are Medium. SPIKES and its process critique come from medical bad-news research, so using them with a manager is an adaptation, and the no-surprises advice (gabarro-kotter-managing-your-boss-03) is expert guidance rather than tested experimentally.

situations.title: Networking at an event
situations.context: You are at a conference reception or industry mixer where you know few people. Many people find networking uncomfortable because it feels transactional, there is no script, and afterward they replay every awkward moment and decide not to follow up. The real value usually comes from follow-up with acquaintances, which is exactly the step most people skip.
situations.goal: A few genuine two-way conversations, at least one person you follow up with, and the sense that you offered something rather than only asked.

approach.step: Decide what you can offer
approach.detail: Before you go, list two or three things you could give: an introduction, a useful article, something you learned, sincere appreciation. Thinking about giving rather than getting makes networking feel less grubby, and social skill is something you can build with practice.

approach.step: Prepare a few topics, not lines
approach.detail: Spend thirty seconds jotting about five topics: something about the event, a session you saw, a question you are curious about. Keep it as a safety net for lulls, not a script; your attention should be on the person in front of you.

approach.step: Open with the setting, then be interested
approach.detail: Start with a question about the shared situation rather than a stock line. When they answer, listen for a detail that genuinely interests you and ask about it.

approach.step: Follow up on their answers instead of turning to yourself
approach.detail: Ask a follow-up before you share your own version, and avoid asking a question just so you can answer it yourself. Once there is some warmth, a question about choices or motives (what drew you to this work?) tends to go further than another fact question.

approach.step: Leave while the energy is still good
approach.detail: When turns get shorter or the topic repeats, signal you need to move on, ask one last question, and close warmly. Ending a little early is better than letting a good conversation run dry.

approach.step: Follow up within a few days
approach.detail: Send the thing you offered, with a short note. You were probably liked more than you think, so do not let a critical replay talk you out of it; acquaintances you are only loosely connected to are often the ones who lead to new opportunities.

example_wording: First time at this conference? I am trying to work out which sessions are worth it.
You mentioned you moved from finance into product. What pulled you over?
I have really enjoyed this. I need to find a colleague before the keynote, but first: what is the one session you would not miss tomorrow?
Good to meet you last night. Here is the article on vendor pricing I mentioned. Hope it is useful.
pitfalls: Leading with your pitch or a request before any real conversation
Asking a question and then using the answer as a cue to talk about yourself
Staying in one conversation until it fizzles out
Replaying the conversation, deciding it went badly, and never following up
Collecting business cards without offering anything
situations.evidence_note: Two steps rest on High-confidence findings: the liking gap (boothby-2018-01) and the value of deeper questions (supercommunicators-05). The rest are Medium, including the large LinkedIn experiment on weak ties (rajkumar-weak-ties-2022-01) and the advice to network to give (king-social-chemistry-02), which is mainly a reframing to reduce discomfort.

situations.title: Apologizing in writing
situations.context: You missed a commitment, sent something hurtful, or made an error that cost a colleague or client, and you need to apologize by email or message. Writing strips out your tone, so the reader fills the gaps, often with the worst reading. The urge to explain what happened can turn the apology into an excuse.
situations.goal: The reader sees that you own what happened, understands the impact you caused, knows what you will do to fix it, and feels the relationship is on firmer ground.

approach.step: Decide whether writing is the right channel
approach.detail: For a serious or emotional rupture, a call or a conversation in person carries tone better than text. Write when the harm happened in writing, the person is remote, or a written record helps, and offer to talk as well.

approach.step: Lead with plain responsibility
approach.detail: Open by naming the specific thing you did and saying it was your fault. Owning it clearly is the single most important part of an apology, ahead of everything else.

approach.step: Name the impact on them
approach.detail: Say what your action cost the other person in concrete terms, so they can see you understand it from their side.

approach.step: Offer a specific repair and a change
approach.detail: Say what you are doing to fix the damage, or ask what would help, and what you will do differently next time. A repair offer is the second most valued part of an apology.

approach.step: Keep it short and warm, without excuses or jokes
approach.detail: Brevity and warmth can pull against each other in writing; resolve it by cutting explanation and padding, not kindness. Any explanation should be one sentence that does not excuse, skip asking for forgiveness, and leave out humor, which makes an admission sound less serious.

approach.step: Reread it as the hurt person before sending
approach.detail: Pause and read each line in a sharper voice than you intended. If any phrase could sound defensive or sarcastic, rewrite it to say your meaning plainly.

approach.step: Follow through, and let trust rebuild over time
approach.detail: Do what you promised and, later, show that you did. After a bigger breach, expect the relationship to warm gradually rather than snap back after one message.

example_wording: I missed Friday's deadline for your section, and that was my fault.
It meant you presented to the client without the numbers, which put you in a hard spot.
The numbers are attached now. From here on, I will flag any risk to a shared deadline at least two days ahead.
If it would help to talk it through, I am free any time this afternoon.
pitfalls: Writing 'sorry if you felt' instead of naming what you did
A long account of what went wrong that reads as an excuse
Pressing for forgiveness or a quick reply
Adding a joke to lighten the mood
Apologizing well and then repeating the same mistake
situations.evidence_note: All supporting insights are Medium. The best evidence is the experimental ranking of apology components (lewicki-apologies-2016-01) and the email tone studies (kruger-epley-2005-01); the gradual-repair step (connect-14) rests mainly on the authors' own experience.

situations.title: Asking for a raise
situations.context: You believe your pay has fallen behind your contribution or the market. Asking feels like a confrontation with someone you depend on, so people go in with a number and no plan, argue from personal need, and back down at the first hesitation. Afterward they often feel they pushed too hard even when they did not.
situations.goal: A fair conversation grounded in clear standards that ends in an increase, or in specific terms and a date for one.

approach.step: Know your alternative before you ask
approach.detail: Work out what you will do if the answer is no: stay and revisit later, pursue an outside offer, or seek a different role. Your best alternative, not a rigid bottom line, is what tells you whether an offer is good enough.

approach.step: Gather fair standards
approach.detail: Collect market data for your role, internal pay bands if available, and concrete evidence of how your scope has grown. Standards that do not depend on either side's will give your manager a legitimate reason to say yes.

approach.step: Think about your manager's interests and limits
approach.detail: You and your manager depend on each other, and they have budget cycles and their own boss to answer to. Consider what they need (keeping a reliable performer, staying within budget) so you can propose something that serves both.

approach.step: Open with a specific, justified number
approach.detail: If you have done your research, name an ambitious but defensible figure and the standard behind it. A first number anchors the conversation, but an extreme one with no reason can backfire.

approach.step: If base pay is stuck, widen the package
approach.detail: Ask what is constraining the answer, then explore other issues together: timing, title, bonus, scope, training. If you disagree about how you will perform, propose a raise tied to a measurable target and date.

approach.step: Do not take it back because it felt uncomfortable
approach.detail: Afterward you may feel you came on too strong; most people who feel that way did not. Check your manager's later behavior before offering any concession to smooth things over.

approach.step: Confirm what was agreed in writing
approach.detail: Send a short summary of the outcome, including any target, amount and review date, and ask your manager to confirm it.

example_wording: I would like to talk about my compensation. Over the past year my role has grown to include the vendor program, and I have looked at what that scope pays in our market.
Based on that data, I am asking for an increase to 92,000.
If base pay is fixed until the next cycle, could we agree in writing to revisit it in June if I hit the renewal target?
I will send a quick note summarizing what we agreed so we are on the same page.
pitfalls: Asking without knowing what you will do if the answer is no
Arguing from personal need or pressure instead of fair standards
Treating salary as the only issue, so a no on base pay ends the conversation
Apologizing or conceding afterward because you think you overstepped
Leaving with a vague 'we will see' and no date
situations.evidence_note: Three steps rest on High-confidence negotiation insights: knowing your alternative (fisher-ury-getting-to-yes-05), focusing on interests (fisher-ury-getting-to-yes-01) and first-offer anchoring (thompson-mind-heart-negotiator-02). The rest are Medium, and none of the research is specific to pay talks with your own manager, so the managing-up insights (gabarro-kotter) supply the relationship context.

situations.title: Negotiating a job offer
situations.context: You have an offer in hand and a short window to respond. Many people accept on the spot for fear the offer will be pulled, or treat salary as the only issue and assume every gain for them is a loss for the employer. Recruiters may also ask questions, such as your current pay, that are hard to answer well.
situations.goal: An accepted offer whose whole package reflects your value, reached in a way that leaves your future manager glad to have hired you.

approach.step: Set your target and walk-away from your alternatives
approach.detail: Know what you will do if this falls through (stay, another offer, keep searching) and set an ambitious target and a walk-away point from that.

approach.step: List every issue, not just salary
approach.detail: Break the offer into its parts: base, signing bonus, start date, title, remote days, review timing, equity, training budget. Rank how much each matters to you.

approach.step: Ask what matters most on their side
approach.detail: Do not assume they want the opposite of you on everything. Ask where they have flexibility and what constraints they face; some issues, like an early start date, may be wins for both.

approach.step: Meet a loaded question with a relevant question
approach.detail: If you are asked something you have a legitimate reason not to answer fully, such as current pay, reply with a sincere, on-topic question instead of refusing or inventing a number. If they have a right to know, answer honestly.

approach.step: Counter with packages backed by standards
approach.detail: Offer two or three packages that are equally good for you and ask which works best for them; their choice shows their priorities. Tie the numbers to market data so your request rests on a reason, not pressure.

approach.step: Bridge disagreements about the future with a contingency
approach.detail: If they doubt you will ramp up as fast as you expect, propose a review at a set date with an increase tied to measurable results.

approach.step: Get the final terms in writing
approach.detail: Ask for the updated offer in writing and check every agreed item is there before you accept.

example_wording: I am excited about this role and want to make it work. Before I respond on the number, where is there flexibility across salary, signing bonus and start date?
I would rather focus on this role than my current one. What range has the team budgeted for this level?
Two ways this could work for me: 128,000 base with the standard bonus, or 120,000 with a 10,000 signing bonus and a pay review at six months. Which fits better on your side?
Thank you. Could you send the updated terms in writing so I can give you a final answer by Thursday?
pitfalls: Accepting on the spot without asking any questions
Settling salary first, then reopening other items one at a time
Opening with an extreme number you cannot justify
Inventing a competing offer or a current salary
Treating the recruiter or hiring manager as an opponent
situations.evidence_note: This is one of the better supported playbooks: four insights are High (fisher-ury-getting-to-yes-05, fisher-ury-getting-to-yes-01, thompson-mind-heart-negotiator-01, thompson-mind-heart-negotiator-02). The question-deflection step (bitterly-schweitzer-deflection-01, Medium) comes from experiments using negotiation scenarios, and contingency terms (thompson-mind-heart-negotiator-04, Medium) are less tested than anchoring.

situations.title: Pushing back on a deadline with your boss
situations.context: Your boss has set a deadline you believe cannot be met at the quality needed, or has added work without moving the date. Challenging a superior is risky, since managers can read pushback as disloyalty, so people agree in the meeting and quietly miss the date, or push back in frustration. Neither gives your boss what they need to decide well.
situations.goal: A realistic agreement on scope, date or resources that your boss chose with full information, with your reputation for commitment intact.

approach.step: Check what really matters about the deadline
approach.detail: Ask what is driving the date and which results matter most. Sometimes the date is fixed but the scope is flexible, or the reverse, and you cannot know without asking.

approach.step: Raise it early, privately, with evidence
approach.detail: Bring it up as soon as you see the risk, one to one, with the specific numbers behind your estimate rather than a general sense of overload.

approach.step: Start from the goal you share
approach.detail: Open with what you are protecting, such as a launch that works or a client you keep. That makes the constraint you are about to name a service to the goal rather than a complaint.

approach.step: State the constraint plainly
approach.detail: Say in one sentence what cannot be done by the date, without an edge or a long apology.

approach.step: Offer a short menu of options
approach.detail: Present two or three workable paths, such as reduced scope, a later date, or extra help, and let your boss choose. A choice among acceptable options gets less resistance than a single demand.

approach.step: If you disagree on the estimate, tie it to what happens
approach.detail: When your boss believes it will take less time than you do, propose keeping the date with an agreed trigger: if a specific dependency slips by a set amount, the date moves.

approach.step: Confirm in writing and do not walk it back
approach.detail: Send a two-line note confirming the chosen option. If you later feel you pushed too hard, remember that people usually overestimate this, and do not give back what you agreed.

example_wording: I want this launch to land well, so I want to flag a risk now rather than on Thursday.
With the security review added, I cannot get all four features done by Friday at the quality we need.

Three ways I see this working: ship features one and two Friday and the rest Wednesday, keep Friday if Dana takes the reporting piece, or move the whole release to Wednesday. Which works best for you?
Thanks. I will send a quick note confirming we are going with the split release.
pitfalls: Agreeing in the meeting and then missing the date
Raising the problem the day before it is due
Describing your workload without offering any options
Apologizing repeatedly or conceding later because you felt pushy
Going around your boss before talking to them directly
situations.evidence_note: Every supporting insight is Medium. The best evidence is the lab and field research on how upward voice is received (morrison-2014-voice-03) and the line-crossing experiments (ames-wazlawek-2014-01); the Positive No (ury-positive-no-01) and managing-your-boss advice are well regarded practitioner guidance rather than tested protocols.

situations.title: Saying no to extra work
situations.context: A colleague, another team or a senior person asks you to take on a project when you are already at capacity. Saying no feels like letting people down or looking like a poor team player, so many people say yes and resent it, or leave the request unanswered until it becomes a bigger problem.
situations.goal: A clear, warm no that protects your priorities, offers something the other person can accept, and leaves the relationship intact.

approach.step: Notice your default trap
approach.detail: Ask yourself whether you usually give in, snap, or avoid answering, and whether that changes with who is asking. Knowing your pattern tells you what to guard against in this conversation.

approach.step: Remind yourself a no stings less than you fear
approach.detail: People who decline consistently overestimate how upset the asker will be and how much the relationship will suffer. If fear of their reaction is the main reason you would say yes, that is worth questioning.

approach.step: Find the yes behind your no
approach.detail: Name what you are protecting: a deadline you own, quality on current work, your team's capacity. This is the reason you will lead with.

approach.step: Take the request seriously before declining
approach.detail: Acknowledge the request and why it matters to them. Accepting that the need is real is different from accepting the work; keep your honest no for the commitment itself.

approach.step: Say the no plainly, then offer a realistic alternative
approach.detail: Thank them for thinking of you, state the no in one sentence framed around your limit rather than their request, and then offer something you can actually do: a smaller piece, a later date, or a referral. For a request you have already decided against and nothing needs negotiating, a short no, a thank-you and a kind close is enough; if pressed, repeat the no rather than adding reasons. With your own manager, keep the alternative.

approach.step: Hold steady afterward
approach.detail: If you feel you came across as harsh, check that against how they actually behave and, if useful, ask a trusted colleague how you came across. Do not reverse a sound decision to repair a rift that may not exist.

example_wording: Thanks for thinking of me for this. It sounds like a project that matters.
I have committed to getting the migration done by month end, so I cannot take on the onboarding redesign right now.
What I can do is review your plan for thirty minutes next week, or put you in touch with Priya, who led the last one.
I would rather give you a clear answer than a slow maybe: I cannot join this quarter. If it comes back in the fall, please ask again.
pitfalls: Replying 'let me think about it' when you already know the answer
Over-explaining or apologizing at length
Saying no with irritation or a lecture
Giving in when they ask a second time
Offering an alternative you cannot actually deliver
situations.evidence_note: All supporting insights are Medium. The strongest are the experiments showing declines hurt less than expected (givi-kirk-2024-01), though they studied social invitations rather than work requests, and the research on misjudging your own assertiveness (ames-wazlawek-2014-01 and -02). The Positive No structure (ury-positive-no-01) is practitioner guidance. The Next Conversation (Medium, practitioner) argues for a bare no without reasons or alternatives, which pulls against the Positive No; the playbook keeps the alternative for work requests and uses the bare no only when nothing needs negotiating.

situations.title: Giving critical feedback to a peer
situations.context: A colleague at your level keeps doing something that hurts your work: talking over you with clients, missing handoffs, taking credit. You have no authority over them and want to keep a good working relationship, so you say nothing, and the irritation grows into a story about who they are.
situations.goal: Your peer understands the specific behavior and its effect, you understand their side, and you agree on a small change to try.

approach.step: Raise it while it is still small
approach.detail: Bring up a pattern soon after a recent example, before it builds into a blowup. Small issues raised early keep the stakes and emotions low.

approach.step: Separate what they did from your guesses about why
approach.detail: Write down the observable behavior, how it affected you, and, separately, what you are assuming about their motives. Plan to speak only about the first two, and turn any trait you dislike into a specific behavior. If you feel strongly, trace the feeling back to the story you are telling yourself and check it against what you actually saw and heard.

approach.step: Set up a private conversation with goodwill
approach.detail: Pick a private moment with enough time and open by saying why the working relationship matters to you, so they are less likely to feel ambushed. Name the one topic and the outcome you hope for, and if they might hear blame, say what you do not mean before what you do.

approach.step: Name the behavior and your real feeling
approach.detail: Describe one recent, specific behavior in neutral terms, then the impact, using a real feeling word rather than 'I feel that you...'. Skip the praise sandwich; it blurs the message. Describe it the way a camera would record it, with no 'always' or 'never'.

approach.step: Stop, ask for their side, and loop it back
approach.detail: Ask how it looks from where they sit, then restate what you heard and check you got it right. You may be missing part of the picture, including your own part in the pattern.

approach.step: Agree on a small experiment
approach.detail: Settle on a concrete change for both of you and a time to check in. Treat it as an invitation the first time; if the issue keeps recurring, it is fair to be more direct about what happens if nothing changes. Before you finish, say who will do what by when, and when you will check in.

example_wording: Do you have fifteen minutes today? I want to talk about how our client calls are going, because I like working with you and want to keep it that way.
In the last two calls, you answered questions the client asked me before I could. I felt sidelined, and I think the client got confused about who owns the account.
I may be missing something. How did those calls look from your side?
Could we try this for the next two calls: whoever is asked answers first, and we compare notes afterward?
pitfalls: Sandwiching the criticism between compliments
Saying 'I feel that you are controlling', which is a judgment, not a feeling
Telling them what they intended
Asking them to change their personality rather than a behavior
Saving up months of examples and delivering them all at once
situations.evidence_note: The core comes from Connect (Medium), which draws on decades of teaching interpersonal skills rather than controlled trials. The step on setting up the conversation uses one Low-confidence insight (how-to-know-a-person-12). The tension between offering feedback as data (connect-04) and naming consequences (think-faster-talk-smarter-10) is handled by escalating only when a pattern recurs.

situations.title: Receiving harsh feedback
situations.context: A manager or colleague tells you, perhaps bluntly, that your work fell short or that you come across badly. Your body reacts before your mind does, and the urge is to explain your intentions or point out what they got wrong. Even badly delivered feedback usually contains something you could not have seen on your own.
situations.goal: You stay composed, understand the specifics, decide later what to do with it, and leave the other person willing to give you feedback again.

approach.step: Steady your body before you respond
approach.detail: Take one or two slow breaths with a longer exhale than inhale. You do not need to answer right away. Let the words drop for a moment before you decide what to pick up, and remind yourself that you can be competent and still have gotten this wrong.

approach.step: Listen for the bottom line
approach.detail: Slow down and take in the whole message, including what they seem worried about, before forming a reply. Ask yourself what they actually want from you. Instead of blaming yourself or them, guess what they needed or were counting on, and check the guess.

approach.step: Thank them and hold off on explaining
approach.detail: Thank them for telling you. Explaining your intentions straight away tends to sound defensive and makes them less likely to be honest next time.

approach.step: Ask for examples and say back what you heard
approach.detail: Ask for a specific instance, then restate the point in your own words and check you got it right. This makes sure you are reacting to what they meant.

approach.step: Accept the impact as real, even if your intent was good
approach.detail: Their experience of your behavior is real data about how you land, even if you meant well. Find the part that is true and say so before adding any context. Acknowledge the impact first; share what you meant only after they feel heard.

approach.step: Decide later, with other views
approach.detail: Separate the feedback (data) from what you will do about it (your decision). Ask one or two people who see your work whether they notice the same pattern.

approach.step: Close the loop
approach.detail: Once you have acted on it, tell the person what you changed and ask whether they have noticed a difference.

example_wording: Thank you for telling me directly. Give me a second to take that in.
Can you walk me through a specific moment from the review meeting?
So what I am hearing is that my answers sound defensive when someone questions the numbers. Is that right?
I took your point about the review meetings and now open with the open questions. Has it looked different from where you sit?
pitfalls: Explaining your intentions before you understand the point
Criticizing them in return
Agreeing to everything just to end the conversation
Dismissing the content because the delivery was poor
Never telling them what you did with it
situations.evidence_note: All supporting insights are Medium, and most come from practitioner books (Connect, Think Faster, Talk Smarter). The antidote to defensiveness (gottman-seven-principles-01) comes from couples research applied here to work, and the outside-eyes step rests on research on misjudging your own assertiveness (ames-wazlawek-2014-02).

situations.title: A tense conflict with your partner
situations.context: A recurring disagreement about chores, money, time or family has flared again and voices are rising. Under stress people reach for criticism, sarcasm, defensiveness or shutting down, and once heart rates climb, nobody can listen. Many couples then either avoid the topic or relive the same fight.
situations.goal: Each of you feels heard, the specific issue is named directly, and you leave with either a practical step or an arrangement you can both live with for now.

approach.step: Work out what kind of problem this is
approach.detail: Ask whether it is a fixable situation or a lasting difference in personality or needs, and how serious it is. Serious, changeable problems need a direct request; lasting differences need ongoing dialogue rather than a win.

approach.step: Be direct about the problem, not about their character
approach.detail: Name the specific situation, how you feel, and what you need. Directness is what gets problems changed; attacking who they are, sulking, or guilt trips do not. One way to say it: what you observed, how you feel, what you need, and one specific request.

approach.step: Loop their view before you defend yours
approach.detail: When your partner pushes back, restate what you heard, including the feeling under it, and ask if you got it right. Find the part of their complaint that is true and say so.

approach.step: Offer repairs early, and accept clumsy ones
approach.detail: A quick 'that came out wrong' or 'can we start over?' can turn the conversation before it escalates. When your partner tries one, take it even if it is awkward.

approach.step: Take a real break if either of you floods
approach.detail: If your pulse is racing or you want to flee or attack, say so and name a time to come back. Spend at least twenty minutes on something calming, not rehearsing the argument, and then return as promised. Earlier, before it gets that far, a slow breath with a long exhale and naming your feeling in a word can stop the climb.

approach.step: Agree a step and a time to revisit
approach.detail: For a fixable issue, settle a practical change. For a lasting difference, agree a temporary arrangement and check in over the following weeks on whether things are actually improving. Name the need each of you is protecting, then look for a strategy that meets both.

approach.step: Build goodwill between arguments
approach.detail: Respond warmly to small everyday bids for attention and say thanks often. Repairs land in a fight largely because of the goodwill built outside it.

example_wording: When the dishes sit until morning, I feel worn out, and I need us to split evenings in a way we both stick to.
Let me check I have it: you feel like I only notice what you have not done, not what you have. Is that it?
I am getting too heated to listen well. Can we stop and pick this up at eight?
That came out wrong. Can I start over?
pitfalls: Opening with 'you always' or 'you never'
Sarcasm, eye-rolling or mockery
Sulking or guilt trips instead of saying what you want
Pushing on while one of you is flooded
Trying to win a lasting difference once and for all
situations.evidence_note: The strongest support is the High-confidence review showing that direct requests drive change (overall-mcnulty-2017-01); Gottman's principles and looping are Medium. The tension between directness and Gottman's warnings about criticism is resolved by being direct about the specific problem while avoiding attacks on character.

situations.title: Supporting a friend who is grieving
situations.context: A friend has lost a parent, partner, pregnancy or someone else close. Fear of saying the wrong thing leads many people to say nothing, or to reach for silver linings and advice that make the grieving person feel unheard. Grief also lasts far longer than the first weeks, when most support fades.
situations.goal: Your friend feels less alone, their feelings are acknowledged rather than managed, and they get the kind of help they actually want for as long as they need it.

approach.step: Reach out, and keep reaching out
approach.detail: Contact them even if you do not know what to say; showing up matters more than finding the right words. Keep sending small, low-pressure messages that need no reply, especially after the first weeks.

approach.step: Name the feeling and let it make sense
approach.detail: Say what you hear, such as exhaustion or anger, and that it makes sense given what happened. Avoid 'at least' and explanations, which quietly tell them how they should feel. Offer your read as a question ('Are you feeling worn out?') and accept corrections.

approach.step: Ask open questions and listen rather than fix
approach.detail: Use what and how questions to let them talk about what is hardest, and hold back advice unless they ask for it. If they do ask, find out what they want to know before offering it.

approach.step: Ask what kind of help they want
approach.detail: Some people want company, some want practical help, some want space. Ask, offer specific things, and check whether now is a good time rather than imposing.

approach.step: Match how visible your help is to their state
approach.detail: When they are very distressed, offer explicit comfort and understanding. Practical help, such as a meal or a school pickup, often works best done quietly as ordinary friendship, without making a production of it.

approach.step: Stay their ordinary friend
approach.detail: Keep doing normal things together and let them give back when they want to, so the friendship does not become one-way care. If you notice signs of self-harm risk, encourage professional help and contact crisis resources.

example_wording: I am so sorry about your dad. I do not have the right words, but I am here.
It makes sense you are exhausted. You have been holding everything together for weeks.
What has been the hardest part this week?
I am dropping off soup on Thursday. No need to answer the door or text back.
pitfalls: Saying 'at least' or 'everything happens for a reason'
Jumping to advice they did not ask for
Disappearing after the funeral
Saying 'let me know if you need anything', which leaves all the work to them
Missing or brushing past signs that they may be at risk
situations.evidence_note: The comfort ladder (high-dillard-2012-01, High) rests on a meta-analysis of comforting messages and anchors the approach. The support-misfire research (rafaeli-gleason-2009-01 and -02) is Medium and comes from diary studies of couples; the presence-over-fixing insight (how-to-know-a-person-10, Medium) rests on one deeply considered personal case.

situations.title: Reconnecting with a friend you drifted from
situations.context: A friend from a previous job, city or life stage has slipped away, and months or years have passed. Reaching out feels awkward: you worry it will seem odd, that they have moved on, or that you need a good reason. Adult friendships also need repeated time together, which no longer happens by default.
situations.goal: You send a warm message, and if they respond, you rebuild a regular rhythm of time together.

approach.step: Send a short note just because
approach.detail: Write a brief message that shows you were thinking of them: a shared memory, a congratulations, a simple hello. People who receive these appreciate them far more than senders expect, especially when the contact comes out of the blue.

approach.step: Name your shared history and leave out requests
approach.detail: Mention something specific you shared and keep favors out of the first message so it reads as warmth. If you genuinely want their view on something, old contacts tend to keep their trust and often bring fresh ideas, so a specific question can be a natural second step.

approach.step: Assume they will be glad to hear from you
approach.detail: People reliably underestimate how much others like them and enjoy their contact. Treat a slow reply as normal, not as a verdict.

approach.step: Suggest one concrete plan
approach.detail: If they reply warmly, say plainly that you would like to see them and propose a specific time and activity. Do not wait for them to make the next move.

approach.step: Make it recurring and relaxed
approach.detail: Closeness grows from many hours of leisure time, not one big catch-up. A standing walk, call or game night lets the hours build up.

approach.step: Share good news, and celebrate theirs
approach.detail: Tell them about good things in your life, not only troubles, and when they share theirs, respond with real interest and questions.

example_wording: I walked past the old bakery on Elm today and thought of our Saturday mornings. Hope you are doing well.
No agenda, just wanted to say hi. I would love to hear what you are up to these days.
It was so good to catch up. Want to make it a regular thing? I am free for a walk the first Sunday of next month.
pitfalls: Waiting for a perfect reason to get in touch
Opening with a long explanation of why you went quiet
Bundling a favor into the first message
Reading a slow reply as rejection
One great catch-up call followed by another year of silence
situations.evidence_note: Two steps rest on High-confidence findings: the liking gap (boothby-2018-01) and responding warmly to good news (gable-2004-01). The core outreach advice (liu-2023-01, 13 experiments) and the hours estimate for friendship (hall-2019-01) are Medium; the dormant ties study (levin-dormant-ties-2011-01) looked at executives seeking advice, so applying it to friendship is an extension.

situations.title: Small talk with a stranger at a work dinner
situations.context: You are seated for two hours next to someone you do not know: a client's colleague, a coworker's partner, a visitor from another office. There is no easy exit, stock questions run dry fast, and you worry about being boring or saying something awkward. Humor feels risky with people whose position and sensitivities you do not know.
situations.goal: A comfortable two-way conversation that finds at least one topic you both enjoy, so you both leave glad you sat together.

approach.step: Prepare a few topics on the way
approach.detail: Take thirty seconds to note about five possible topics, mixing light ones with a couple that invite real stories, such as something you are both connected to or a question you are curious about.

approach.step: Open with something you both can see
approach.detail: Start with a question about the setting, the event or the food rather than 'what do you do?'. It gives both of you something easy to build on.

approach.step: Follow up on what they say, and do not boomerask
approach.detail: Ask a follow-up about a detail in their answer before offering your own story, and do not ask a question just so you can answer it yourself.

approach.step: Climb when something sparks
approach.detail: Small talk is the starting point, not the problem. When a topic lights them up, move toward their choices, values and experiences; deeper questions feel less awkward than people expect. Go one step at a time and match how much they open up.

approach.step: Keep it light and inclusive
approach.detail: Laugh at their humor, use callbacks to earlier topics, and keep jokes aimed at the situation or yourself. Avoid teasing anyone with less power or anyone who is not there.

approach.step: Switch topics before they go stale
approach.detail: When you notice longer pauses, repeated points or uneasy laughter, change topic confidently, or go back to something earlier that deserved more time.

example_wording: Have you been here before? I am trying to decide whether this menu is ambitious or just long.
You said you coach your daughter's soccer team. How did you end up doing that?
What has been the best part of your year so far, work or otherwise?
Going back to your move from Denver: what do you miss most?
pitfalls: Running through a list of factual questions like an interview
Turning every answer into a story about yourself
Staying on weather and traffic all evening
Teasing someone junior or someone who is not at the table
Jumping to very personal topics before they have opened up at all
situations.evidence_note: The climb toward deeper talk rests on two High-confidence insights (how-to-know-a-person-04 and supercommunicators-05); the rest are Medium. The tension between going deep and climbing gradually (talk-wood-brooks-03) is resolved by starting light and moving up as the other person responds.

situations.title: Presenting to executives
situations.context: You have fifteen minutes on a leadership agenda to get a decision or funding. Executives are short on time, interrupt, and skip ahead, while you know the material so well that you naturally start with background and detail. Nerves are highest in the first minute, exactly when you need to land the main point.
situations.goal: The executives grasp your recommendation in the first minute, see why it matters to them, and make or schedule the decision.

approach.step: Clarify audience and intent, then find the one-sentence core
approach.detail: Write who is in the room, what they care about, and the action you want from them. Then reduce your message to one sentence they could repeat, and cut points that compete with it. A message map (one headline, about three supporting points, evidence under each) gives you the 15-second, two-minute and full versions from one plan.

approach.step: Open with the answer, framed briefly
approach.detail: Skip the agenda and history. Give a sentence of situation, a sentence of what has changed, and then your recommendation.

approach.step: Group your support under the main point
approach.detail: Give two to four reasons that answer 'why?' or 'how?', each with its evidence. Make each slide title a full-sentence takeaway and keep the slide to one message.

approach.step: Make the key number land in plain terms
approach.detail: Translate the most important figure into a comparison the audience can picture, and strip out internal jargon you no longer notice.

approach.step: Rehearse the first minute and do a dry run
approach.detail: Practice your opening sentences aloud until they are automatic, since that is when nerves spike. Do a full rehearsal with a colleague a few days before and ask for one or two specific changes. For a high-stakes briefing, rehearse aloud on separate days, record one run, and keep going until it sounds conversational rather than recited.

approach.step: End on the decision you need
approach.detail: Script your last sentence so it states the decision and the timing. Do not end on a 'Questions?' slide; restate the recommendation and move into discussion.

example_wording: I am asking for approval to move customer support to a 24-hour model starting in Q3.
Today we answer customers in a median of nine hours; our two largest competitors answer in under one, and three of last quarter's lost renewals cited response time.
Put simply, waiting costs us about one renewal a month.
The decision I need today is a yes on the pilot budget, or a date when you can give one.
pitfalls: Opening with background, methodology or the agenda
Slides full of paragraphs that compete with you
Presenting every point you worked on instead of the few that matter
Raw numbers with no comparison
Ending on a 'Questions?' slide with no clear ask
situations.evidence_note: All supporting insights are Medium, and most come from practitioner methods (Minto, Schramm, the Heaths) that are widely used but not tested as a package. The first-minute rehearsal step rests on research into how speaking anxiety peaks at the start (bodie-2010-02).

situations.title: Handling a hostile question in Q&A
situations.context: After your talk, someone asks a pointed or loaded question, perhaps implying your numbers cannot be trusted or that you are hiding something. Adrenaline pushes you to defend, ramble or dodge. The audience is judging how you handle it at least as much as what you say.
situations.goal: You stay composed, answer the real question honestly and briefly, and keep the trust of the room.

approach.step: Prepare answers to the questions you dread
approach.detail: List the hardest questions you could get and practice short, direct answers aloud until they come out smoothly. A fluent answer is judged far more favorably than a halting one.

approach.step: Breathe and hear the whole question
approach.detail: Take a slow breath and let the person finish. Listen for the concern underneath the wording. A pause of one to four seconds before you answer reads as deliberate, not stuck.

approach.step: Restate the question in neutral words
approach.detail: Paraphrase it without the loaded language. This confirms what is being asked, buys you a moment to think, and lets the room hear a fair version of the question.

approach.step: Answer it directly, with one example and why it matters
approach.detail: Give your answer in one clear sentence, add one concrete example or data point, and say why it matters to the person asking. Answer the question that was asked; listeners who keep the question in mind will notice a dodge.

approach.step: Turn attacks toward the problem
approach.detail: If the question is personal or angry, treat it as a chance to understand a concern rather than a threat. Recast the attack as the shared problem and ask what would address it.

approach.step: Use a question back only when withholding is legitimate
approach.detail: If the question asks for something you genuinely should not disclose, a sincere, relevant question of your own works better than refusing. If they have a right to know, answer honestly or say you do not know and will follow up.

example_wording: The question is whether these numbers are more reliable than last year's forecast. That is a fair question.
Yes, they are. This year's figures come from signed contracts, not pipeline estimates; 80 percent of the Q2 total is already invoiced. That means you can plan hiring against it with much less risk.
I hear the frustration about last year, and I share it. What would you need to see to feel confident in the next forecast?
I do not know the regional split off the top of my head. I will send it to everyone by Friday.
pitfalls: Repeating the hostile wording when you restate the question
Smoothly answering a different, easier question
Arguing with the person who asked
A long defensive answer that buries the point
Bluffing when you do not know
situations.evidence_note: All supporting insights are Medium. The research on how audiences judge answers (rogers-norton-artful-dodger-01 and -02) and the deflection experiments (bitterly-schweitzer-deflection-01) give the best evidence; the reframing of attacks (fisher-ury-getting-to-yes-06) comes from negotiation and is adapted here to Q&A.

situations.title: Being put on the spot in a meeting
situations.context: In the middle of a meeting, a senior person turns to you: what do you think, or where are we on this? You did not prepare, your mind goes blank or races, and you are tempted either to ramble through everything you know or to apologize. The moment feels like a test, which makes it harder.
situations.goal: A short, clear and useful answer within a few seconds, or an honest holding answer with a specific follow-up.

approach.step: Take one slow breath
approach.detail: Breathe in briefly and out for longer. A one or two second pause is normal and reads as thoughtful.

approach.step: Drop the goal of a perfect answer
approach.detail: Aim to be clear and useful, not impressive, and treat the question as a chance to help rather than a test. Trying to be brilliant uses up the mental capacity you need to respond.

approach.step: Check what is really being asked
approach.detail: Listen for what the person actually needs from you. If it is unclear, paraphrase the question; that also buys a moment to think.

approach.step: Answer in What, So What, Now What
approach.detail: Give the key point, why it matters to the people in the room, and the next step or recommendation.

approach.step: Cut it to what they need
approach.detail: Lead with the answer, skip jargon and backstory, and offer more detail only if they want it.

approach.step: If you blank, reset without apologizing
approach.detail: Restate your last point or the question to find your footing, and skip 'sorry, I am nervous'; others notice far less than you feel. If you do not have the answer, say when you will get it.

approach.step: Review it briefly afterward, then let it go
approach.detail: Look back using your own name or 'you', as if coaching a friend: what worked, and one thing to try next time. Then stop replaying it.

example_wording: So you are asking whether we can still hit the date if the vendor slips. Is that right?
Short answer: yes, with one change. The vendor only affects reporting, so a slip delays reports but not the launch. I suggest we decide by Friday whether to launch without them.
I want to give you an accurate number rather than a guess. I will send it by three today.
pitfalls: Apologizing for being unprepared or nervous
Starting with the backstory instead of the answer
Answering before you understand the question
Trying to say everything you know
Bluffing a number you are not sure of
situations.evidence_note: All supporting insights are Medium. Most come from one practitioner book (Think Faster, Talk Smarter); the two research-based steps are the illusion of transparency (savitsky-gilovich-2003-01) and distanced self-talk (kross-2014-01), both from experiments.

situations.title: Writing an email that needs a decision
situations.context: You need a busy person, such as your manager, another team's lead or a client, to choose or approve something by a date. Busy readers skim, put things off, or never reply when a message looks like work. The instinct is to write a long, careful email with all the context, which makes the decision harder to find.
situations.goal: The reader sees what you need in the first lines and replies with a decision quickly.

approach.step: Name the one decision and who it is for
approach.detail: Before writing, state who the reader is, what they care about, and the single response you need. If you have several asks, send the others later.

approach.step: Put the ask and the deadline on top
approach.detail: Put the decision and the date in the subject line and first sentence, so someone reading only those knows what you need. Give a real deadline and why it matters, not vague urgency.

approach.step: Make answering take seconds
approach.detail: Offer numbered options so they can reply with a number, mark your recommendation, and say what you will do by default if you do not hear back.

approach.step: Give only the reasons they need
approach.detail: Support your recommendation with a few grouped points, and cut ideas that are merely nice to know. Move background to the end or an attachment.

approach.step: Format lightly for skimmers
approach.detail: Use short paragraphs and a list for the options. Emphasize only the one most important line; when everything is bold, nothing stands out.

approach.step: Edit for active, brief and clear, then reread on a phone
approach.detail: Put the person doing the action first, delete filler, and read the email once as the recipient would on a small screen.

example_wording: Subject: Decision needed by Thursday: vendor for the Q3 survey
Hi Sam, I need your pick between two vendors by Thursday so we can sign before their pricing changes on the 1st.
Reply 1 or 2. 1: Northfield, 18,000, ready in four weeks (my recommendation). 2: Cobalt, 14,000, ready in seven weeks, which puts results after the board meeting.
Details on both are below. If I have not heard by Thursday noon, I will go with Northfield.
pitfalls: Opening with background and burying the ask in paragraph four
Asking for three decisions in one email
Ending with an open 'thoughts?' instead of a question they can answer quickly
No deadline, or a false 'urgent'
Bolding so much that nothing stands out
situations.evidence_note: The strongest support is the High-confidence field experiments showing shorter messages get more action (rogers-busy-readers-02). The other Writing for Busy Readers insights and the email urgency research (giurge-bohns-2021-01) are Medium; Schramm's and Minto's structures are practitioner methods.

situations.title: Running a meeting that wanders
situations.context: You lead a recurring meeting that runs over time, drifts into tangents and complaints, and ends without clear decisions. As the person running it you probably rate it more highly than attendees do. Steering people back feels rude, so the drift continues.
situations.goal: Meetings that answer specific questions, finish on time, and end with decisions, owners and deadlines.

approach.step: Check whether the meeting needs to exist, and who needs to be there
approach.detail: Ask what the meeting must produce and whether that needs live discussion. Invite only people needed to answer the questions, and give others a graceful way to send input instead of attending.

approach.step: Write the agenda as questions, with time for each
approach.detail: Turn each item into a question the group must answer, such as 'Which two vendors do we shortlist?', and estimate time per question. Book a little less time than the default. For any question that ends in a decision, say up front how it will be made: command, consult, vote or consensus.

approach.step: Open as a host
approach.detail: Start on time, thank people for coming, and state the questions and the end time.

approach.step: Bring tangents back to the purpose
approach.detail: Acknowledge a tangent briefly, park it, and return to the question on the table. If the purpose itself turns out to be wrong, change it openly rather than drifting.

approach.step: Turn complaints into specific problems
approach.detail: When someone says nothing ever works, acknowledge the frustration, then ask what the specific problem is and who could change it. Catch it early; complaining spreads.

approach.step: Gather ideas silently before discussing
approach.detail: When you need ideas, give everyone a few minutes to write their own first, then pool and discuss. This gets more ideas and stops the group anchoring on the loudest or most senior voice.

approach.step: Close each question with an answer, an owner and a date
approach.detail: State the decision aloud before moving on, and send decisions and owners to everyone soon after the meeting. Make each owner one named person and agree how progress will be checked.

example_wording: Thanks for coming. We have three questions to answer and we will be done at 10:25.
Good point, and it is not today's question. I will park it and we will come back to which vendors to shortlist.
It sounds like the approval process is frustrating everyone. What is the specific step slowing us down, and who could change it?
So: vendors A and C, Jamal owns the outreach, and he will report back Monday.
pitfalls: An agenda of topic labels instead of questions
Letting the meeting fill the whole calendar slot
Cutting tangents off harshly, or not at all
Open brainstorming where the most senior person speaks first
No written record of decisions and owners
situations.evidence_note: Two steps rest on High-confidence meeting science: the before, during and after checklist (mroz-allen-2018-meetings-01) and silent brainstorming (rogelberg-meetings-05). The other Rogelberg insights and the complaining-spiral finding are Medium, and steering back to purpose (improv-wisdom-08) is practitioner guidance.

situations.title: Presenting on a video call
situations.context: You are presenting to a remote group with your slides shared, faces reduced to small tiles or turned off. You get little feedback, cannot read the room, and may find yourself watching your own face. Video is also tiring for everyone, which cuts how much people speak up.
situations.goal: The audience follows your structure, engages and asks questions, and nobody leaves the call drained.

approach.step: Set up your frame, then hide self-view
approach.detail: Check lighting and framing at the start, then turn off self-view so you are not watching yourself. Sit far enough back that you can gesture naturally.

approach.step: Plan participation that does not depend on cameras
approach.detail: Make cameras optional and plan other ways in: inviting people by name, chat, and pauses for questions. Replace the cues video loses with explicit verbal ones rather than demanding more nonverbal effort from everyone.

approach.step: Signal your structure out loud and on screen
approach.detail: Say how many points you have and number them as you go, and give the key points one consistent visual cue on your slides.

approach.step: Deliver key thoughts to the lens
approach.detail: For your most important sentences, look at the camera, delivering one complete thought before glancing back at notes or slides.

approach.step: Check understanding by asking, not by reading faces
approach.detail: Small video cues are unreliable, and silence is not agreement. Ask for their version of the main point or next step, framed as checking your own explanation.

approach.step: Follow up in writing and review the recording
approach.detail: Send a short written summary of decisions and next steps after the call. If you recorded it, watch it once with sound only and once with picture only, and pick one or two changes.

example_wording: Cameras are optional today, and the chat is open the whole time.
Three changes to cover; I will number them as we go. The first is...
Before I move on: Priya, does this match what your team is seeing? Anyone else, drop a question in chat.
To make sure I explained it well, what is the one change you would take back to your team?
pitfalls: Requiring everyone's camera on for the whole session
Reading the slides aloud
Watching your own face instead of the content and the camera
Taking silence as understanding
Running an hour without a break or a change of pace
situations.evidence_note: The video-fatigue research (bailenson-zoom-fatigue-01) and the camera-optional field experiment (shockley-camera-fatigue-01) are Medium, as are signaling and understanding checks. The thin-channel advice (communicate-with-mastery-12) is Low and not confirmed in its book; it is used only for explicit participation and a written follow-up, and the library has no dedicated source on presenting virtually.

situations.title: Persuading a skeptical colleague
situations.context: You want a peer or another team's lead to adopt a new process or tool, and they have resisted. You have no authority over them. The natural move is another meeting and more arguments, which tends to make people dig in.
situations.goal: The colleague agrees to try a small version, or you understand the real obstacle; either way the relationship stays strong.

approach.step: Ask why they have not changed already
approach.detail: Before pushing, find out what is holding them back: feeling pushed, attachment to the current way, too big a leap, risk, or not enough proof. Ask them directly rather than guessing.

approach.step: Listen fully and reflect their view
approach.detail: Let them explain how they came to their position without interrupting or rebutting, then reflect it back, including their reluctance. Being heard well tends to loosen fixed views; arguing hardens them.

approach.step: Draw out their own reasons for change
approach.detail: Ask questions that invite their reasons, such as what would be better if approvals were faster, and reflect any statement that leans toward change. People are persuaded more by reasons they say themselves.

approach.step: Frame it in their values and currencies
approach.detail: Connect your proposal to what they care about and how they are measured, such as audit safety, their team's time, or recognition, not to the reasons that convinced you.

approach.step: Make the first step small, safe and reversible
approach.detail: Propose a time-bound pilot with an easy way back and agreed criteria for judging it. Build from one accepted step to the next rather than asking for the whole change at once.

approach.step: Turn a yes into specifics
approach.detail: When they agree, settle who does what by when, confirm it in writing, and set a check-in. A yes in the room does not always become action; judge success by what gets done.

example_wording: You have kept the spreadsheet process for good reasons. What would we lose if we switched?
So the worry is that the new tool hides the audit trail your team needs at quarter end. Did I get that right?
What would be different for your team if approvals took a day instead of a week?
What if we ran just next month's approvals through it, kept the spreadsheet as backup, and reviewed the results together on the 30th?
pitfalls: Answering every objection with a stronger argument
Making the case in your own values ('it is more modern')
Asking for the full rollout up front
Dismissing their concern as resistance to change
Counting a yes in the meeting as done
situations.evidence_note: Three insights are High: letting people voice their own reasons (miller-rollnick-mi-2023-01), asking rather than imagining their view (how-to-know-a-person-06), and the finding that a yes does not always mean follow-through (feeley-anker-aloe-2012-01). The rest are Medium; motivational interviewing comes from counseling, so using it with colleagues is an adaptation.

situations.title: Setting a boundary with a family member
situations.context: A sibling, in-law or other relative keeps doing something that crosses a line for you: dropping by unannounced, overriding your parenting, calling during work. Long history and fear of a rift make it hard to say anything, so people hint, sulk or put up with it until they explode.
situations.goal: The limit is stated clearly and kindly, the other person knows what you need and what you will do, and they hear that you value the relationship.

approach.step: Name the expectation and your usual pattern
approach.detail: Pin down exactly which expectation is being stretched. Notice whether you usually give in, snap or avoid, and whether a cycle of avoiding, then exploding, then feeling guilty has set in.

approach.step: Find your yes and draft your no
approach.detail: Identify what you are protecting, such as your family's routines or your workday, and write the request as one plain sentence about the behavior, not the person.

approach.step: Open by affirming the relationship
approach.detail: Say what you value about them and the relationship before raising the limit, so they can hear it as a way to stay close.

approach.step: State the limit directly, as your need
approach.detail: Name the specific behavior, its effect on you, and the change you are asking for. Hints, sulking and guilt can win brief reassurance but leave the problem in place. Say it as an 'I' sentence about what you will do, and name a proportionate consequence if it continues.

approach.step: Offer a yes they can accept
approach.detail: Propose what you can welcome instead: a different time, a way to raise concerns, a role you would love them to play.

approach.step: Expect less fallout than you fear, and hold steady
approach.detail: People usually overestimate how hurt the other person will be. If you feel you went too far, look at how they actually behave before backing down. If the limit is crossed, carry out the consequence calmly each time; a consequence you do not enforce teaches people the boundary is optional.

approach.step: Agree when to revisit
approach.detail: Treat the boundary as something you can adjust as circumstances change, and name a time to check how it is going.

example_wording: I love how involved you are with the kids, and I want you to stay close to them.
I need decisions about bedtime and screens to stay with us, so I am asking you not to change them when you babysit.
If you have concerns, tell me privately and I will really listen.
Can we check in after the holidays and see how it is going?
pitfalls: Hinting or sulking and hoping they work it out
Framing the limit as a verdict on their character
Backing down at the first sign of hurt
Justifying the request at great length
Delivering an ultimatum in the heat of an argument
situations.evidence_note: All supporting insights are Medium. The research pieces (overall-mcnulty-2017-02 on guilt trips, givi-kirk-2024-01 on declines, ames-wazlawek-2014-01 on feeling you overstepped) come from couples, invitations and negotiations, so applying them to other family members is an extension; Connect and Ury supply the structure. The consequence and follow-through steps come from The Next Conversation (Medium, practitioner advice without a direct test).

situations.title: A first conversation with a new manager
situations.context: You have a new manager, either because they joined or you did, and your first one-to-one sets the tone. You do not yet know their priorities, how they like to work, or how they want bad news. The temptation is to spend the time impressing them, or to wait passively for them to define everything.
situations.goal: You leave knowing their top priorities, how they want updates and bad news, and what you can decide alone, and they know what you need to do your best work.

approach.step: Prepare by thinking about their world
approach.detail: Note what you know of their goals and the pressures they face from above, and list what each of you needs from the other. The relationship runs on mutual dependence.

approach.step: Jot down your goals for the conversation
approach.detail: Write a few things you want to learn and one or two you want them to know. State them early and ask what they want from the meeting too.

approach.step: Ask about priorities, updates, decisions and bad news
approach.detail: Ask directly which results matter most, how often and in what format they want updates, which decisions you can make alone, and how they want to hear about problems.

approach.step: Ask one bigger question and follow up
approach.detail: Add an open question about what success looks like to them, and ask follow-ups about the most alive part of the answer rather than moving through a checklist.

approach.step: Share a little about yourself and what you need
approach.detail: Offer something slightly beyond small talk, such as what helps you do your best work or a concern about the role, and see whether they reciprocate. A modest step builds trust; a big disclosure in a first meeting can feel like too much.

approach.step: Summarize in writing and confirm
approach.detail: Send a short recap of what you heard about priorities and ways of working, and ask them to correct anything you missed.

example_wording: What are the two or three results that matter most to you this quarter?
How do you like to get updates: a short written note before we talk, or talking it through?
If something is going wrong, when and how do you want to hear about it?
One thing that helps me do my best work is hearing early when priorities shift. I will send a short recap of what we covered today.
pitfalls: Spending the meeting reciting your accomplishments
Guessing their preferences instead of asking
Only closed, factual questions
Sharing nothing about yourself, or far too much
Never revisiting expectations as things change
situations.evidence_note: All supporting insights are Medium. The managing-your-boss advice is expert guidance rather than experimental findings; the disclosure steps reconcile a noted tension between stretching modestly (connect-02) and opening up to invite trust (supercommunicators-08) by taking a small step and watching the response.

situations.title: Responding when someone shares good news
situations.context: Your partner gets a promotion, a friend gets engaged, a sibling finally sells their house. It seems easy, but people often reply distractedly, jump to a downside, or turn the talk to their own news. When the news touches a sore spot for you, it is even harder to respond well.
situations.goal: The person feels celebrated and gets to relive the moment, and the relationship grows stronger.

approach.step: Stop and turn toward them
approach.detail: Put the phone down and give them your attention. Sharing news is a bid for connection, and how you respond in that moment matters.

approach.step: Show real pleasure
approach.detail: Let your words and tone show you are glad. A quiet 'that's nice' lands as indifference.

approach.step: Ask questions that let them relive it
approach.detail: Ask how it happened, what the moment was like, and what it means to them, and follow up on the details.

approach.step: Name what it says about them
approach.detail: Point to the effort or quality behind the success, specifically. Sincere compliments land better than people expect.

approach.step: Hold concerns for another day
approach.detail: If you have worries, such as longer hours or a move, save them for a later conversation unless they ask.

approach.step: If it touches a sore spot, be glad and honest
approach.detail: If the news is hard for you, lead with real gladness, name your own difficulty briefly, and keep the focus on them. Come back later with full interest.

example_wording: Wait, you got it? That is fantastic. Tell me everything.
What was it like when they called?
You have been working toward this for two years. All those early mornings paid off.
I am really happy for you, and it is a little hard for me too after my own year. Mostly I am just proud of you.
pitfalls: 'That's nice' while still looking at your screen
Jumping straight to the downside
Turning the conversation to your own news
Faking enthusiasm and then quietly pulling away
situations.evidence_note: The core is well supported: active-constructive responding (gable-2004-01) and giving compliments (talk-wood-brooks-10) are both High. The sore-spot step relies on a Low-confidence insight (franco-platonic-03) and is offered as an option when wholehearted enthusiasm would be fake.

situations.title: Talking across a political disagreement
situations.context: A relative or friend holds a view on a charged issue that you strongly disagree with, and it comes up at dinner. Views like these are tied to identity, so facts and arguments tend to harden them. These conversations usually escalate or get avoided, and both leave a residue.
situations.goal: Both of you feel understood and the conversation stays respectful; any shift in views is a small bonus, not the aim.

approach.step: Aim for understanding, not conversion
approach.detail: Decide beforehand that success is mutual understanding. Even good stories and conversations move views only modestly, so hoping to win sets you up to push too hard. First ask whether the two of you actually need to agree on this, and whether you need to agree now.

approach.step: Ask how they came to their view, and listen
approach.detail: Invite them to explain their view as a story of how they got there, and listen without rebutting. Being well listened to tends to make people's views more nuanced.

approach.step: Loop and acknowledge what you share
approach.detail: Restate their view and the feeling under it until they confirm, then name a specific point you agree with.

approach.step: Notice what layer you differ on
approach.detail: Ask yourself whether you disagree about facts, feelings, goals or identity. If the issue is tied to who they are, acknowledge that identity and look for one you share, such as fellow parents or neighbors.

approach.step: Trade stories, not just arguments
approach.detail: Ask about a relevant experience in their life, then share a short, concrete story of your own that explains your view.

approach.step: Speak with visible openness
approach.detail: Hedge your claims, avoid lecturing, say what you are for rather than only what you oppose, and if you add an argument, frame it in values they hold. Say 'I see it differently' rather than 'you're wrong'.

example_wording: I see this really differently, and I would like to understand how you got to where you are. What shaped your view?
So for you this is mostly about keeping the town safe for your kids. Is that right?
I think you are right that the current system is not working for anyone.
Can I tell you what happened to my neighbor last year? It is a big part of why I see it the way I do.
pitfalls: Unloading facts and statistics
Talking about 'people like you' or 'your side'
Trying to win in one conversation
Sarcasm or mockery
Avoiding the topic entirely while resentment builds
situations.evidence_note: Two High-confidence insights anchor this: field experiments on exchanging stories (kalla-broockman-2020-01) and the meta-analysis showing stories nudge rather than convert (braddock-dillard-2016-01), which sets realistic expectations. The listening, receptiveness and identity insights are Medium.

situations.title: Recovering when a joke lands badly
situations.context: In a meeting or a team chat, you made a joke that drew silence, or a colleague later tells you it stung. It is hard to tell a harmless flop from real hurt, and the reflex is to defend your intent. Your position matters: a joke from someone senior can land very differently than you think.
situations.goal: You tell a flop from harm, repair any harm quickly and specifically, and use humor with better judgment from then on.

approach.step: Tell a flop from harm
approach.detail: A joke that simply falls flat costs little and is best left alone. A joke that hurt someone needs to be addressed, even if nobody objected in the moment.

approach.step: If it was a flop, move on
approach.detail: Do not explain the joke or apologize at length; return to the topic. A plain flop says little about your judgment.

approach.step: If it hurt, thank them and own it
approach.detail: When someone tells you, thank them, accept that a line was crossed, and do not defend your intent or suggest they are too sensitive.

approach.step: Apologize specifically and briefly
approach.detail: Name what you said, its effect on them, and what you will do differently. If the joke was public, consider whether the correction should be public too.

approach.step: Work out why it hurt
approach.detail: Check the joke against truth, pain and distance: would the plain statement be acceptable, how raw is the topic, is it yours to joke about? Also ask whether the target had less power than you.

approach.step: Be extra careful with humor in writing
approach.detail: Sarcasm and teasing are misread in text far more often than writers expect. In chat, drop jokes that depend on tone, and take any apology or correction to a private message or a call.

example_wording: Thanks for telling me. You are right, that crossed a line, and I am sorry.
I joked about your spreadsheet error in front of the whole team, and it made you look careless to people you work with. I will not do that again.
After a flop, simply: Anyway, back to the timeline.
pitfalls: Saying 'it was just a joke' or 'you are too sensitive'
Apologizing at length for a harmless flop
Explaining why the joke was funny
Making the same joke again in a chat thread
Taking laughter from junior colleagues as proof the joke was fine
situations.evidence_note: All supporting insights are Medium. Most come from Humor, Seriously, whose authors have an interest in stressing humor's benefits; the apology research (lewicki-apologies-2016-01) and the email tone experiments (kruger-epley-2005-01) add independent support.

situations.title: Calming nerves before a high-stakes talk
situations.context: You have a big presentation, interview or pitch coming up, and the dread starts days before. On the day your heart races just as you begin. Telling yourself to calm down rarely works, and the belief that everyone can see your nerves makes them worse.
situations.goal: You walk in with your nerves working for you, a solid first minute, and a plan to grow steadily less afraid over time.
